Projecting onto the top side joins two nodes when they share a neighbor below, weighted by how many they share: A-B and A-C share only E (accent), B-D and C-D share only F (teal), and B-C shares both, so it is a plain edge of weight 2." width="100%"} A projection turns a two-mode network (e.g. people and the events they attend) into a one-mode network of just one kind of node (people linked to people). Two nodes in the chosen partition become connected if they share at least one neighbor in the other partition, and the edge weight equals the number of shared neighbors. The partitions are those returned by `bipartite_sets()`. Projections are the standard way to analyze bipartite data with ordinary one-mode tools (centrality, community detection, etc.). Typical examples: - co-authorship networks from author-paper data - gene-gene networks from gene-disease associations (genes linked by shared diseases) - product similarity from customer purchase data The result is a *new* graph; the original graph is left unchanged. The projection is always undirected and weighted. Each node keeps its ID, label and attributes from the original graph; the edges are new, so they get fresh IDs. Nodes of the chosen partition that share no neighbor with any other node still appear, as isolated nodes. Note that projections can be much denser than the original graph: a node in the other partition with *d* neighbors creates up to *d(d - 1)/2* projected edges. On directed graphs edge direction is ignored, both for the partitioning and for which nodes count as shared neighbors. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [which]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which partition to project onto: `0` (default) for the first set returned by `bipartite_sets()` or `1` for the second. In each connected component, partition `0` is the side containing the component's lowest node ID, so it's often clearest to look up the partition that holds a known node (see the examples). Any other value raises an error. [weighting]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["count"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : How projected edges are weighted, for nodes `u` and `v` with neighbor sets `N(u)` and `N(v)` in the other partition: - `"count"` (default): the number of shared neighbors, `|N(u) & N(v)|` - `"collaboration"`: Newman's collaboration weight, the sum over shared neighbors `n` of `1 / (deg(n) - 1)`, so a shared paper with many authors counts for less - `"jaccard"`: `|N(u) & N(v)| / |N(u) | N(v)|` - `"overlap"`: `|N(u) & N(v)| / min(|N(u)|, |N(v)|)` These match NetworkX's `weighted_projected_graph`, `collaboration_weighted_projected_graph` and `overlap_weighted_projected_graph` (with `jaccard=True` and `jaccard=False`). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected, weighted graph containing only the nodes of the chosen partition, with edges weighted as chosen by `weighting=`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not bipartite, `which=` is not `0` or `1`, or `weighting=` is unknown. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Project a gene-disease network onto genes; genes become connected if they share diseases. "Gene2" shares a disease with each of the other genes, while "Gene1" and "Gene3" share none, so the projection has three nodes but only two edges: ::: {#ba32fde1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["Gene1", "Gene2", "Gene3", "Disease1", "Disease2"]) .add_edges( [ ("Gene1", "Disease1"), ("Gene2", "Disease1"), ("Gene2", "Disease2"), ("Gene3", "Disease2"), ] ) ) set_a, set_b = graph.bipartite_sets() # Find which set contains the genes gene1_id = graph.get_id_from_label("Gene1") gene_set = 0 if gene1_id in set_a else 1 projection = graph.bipartite_projection(which=gene_set) projection.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['Gene1--Gene2', 'Gene2--Gene3'] ``` ::: ::: Edge weights count the shared neighbors. "Ann" and "Bob" attended all three events together, so their edge has weight `3.0`, while each of their links to "Cal" (who only went to the "Fair") has weight `1.0`: ::: {#e323c73e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} events = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Cal", "Gala", "Expo", "Fair"]) .add_edges( [ ("Ann", "Gala"), ("Bob", "Gala"), ("Ann", "Expo"), ("Bob", "Expo"), ("Cal", "Fair"), ("Ann", "Fair"), ("Bob", "Fair"), ] ) ) people = events.bipartite_projection(which=0) { (people.get_label_from_id(s), people.get_label_from_id(t)): people.get_edge(e).weight for e, s, t in people.get_edges_as_tuples() } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {('Ann', 'Bob'): 3.0, ('Ann', 'Cal'): 1.0, ('Bob', 'Cal'): 1.0} ``` ::: ::: Projecting onto the other partition instead links events that share attendees: ::: {#4766603c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} events.bipartite_projection(which=1).get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['Gala--Expo', 'Gala--Fair', 'Expo--Fair'] ``` ::: :::
